Project 05 · dark-matter substructure from strong lensing

Dark Matter Lab

Two instruments. Above: drag a galaxy behind a lens and watch its light bend into arcs; add a dark subhalo, then a small distortion of the lens galaxy, and compare what each does to the arc. Below: half a million dark-matter particles falling into the cosmic web.

What you are looking at

Every pixel is a light ray shot backwards through the lens equation β = θ − α(θ): the pixel's position θ on the sky, minus the deflection α produced by the lens galaxy's mass, gives the point β on the background galaxy whose light lands there. Where many θ map to the same β you get multiple images; where the mapping folds, the pale line marks the critical curve, and the arcs pile up along it. Coordinates are in arcseconds; the box is 6″ across — an HST frame at this scale is about 120 pixels wide.

The confounder problem

Switch to Residual and turn on a subhalo: the view shows the image with the perturbation minus the image without it — the ~1% distortion a detector has to find. Now remove the subhalo and raise the multipole amplitude to 2–3% of θE: the lens galaxy is slightly boxy instead of a perfect ellipse. The residual pattern has the same scale, the same location on the arc, and often the same sign structure.

This is why Lange et al. (2024) watched a JWST subhalo's Bayes factor fall from 60 to 11 once multipoles were fitted, and why O'Riordan (2025) found a 3% multipole erases the population signal. Measuring how often each published method mistakes one for the other is the paper.

What an image cannot tell you

Slide λ. With Rescale source on, nothing changes — every image position and shape is identical although the lens now has a different mass profile and the source a different size. That is the mass-sheet degeneracy: imaging alone fixes the mass only up to this one-parameter family. Turn the rescaling off and the images move, because you have broken the degeneracy by hand — real data cannot.

Subhalo mass is quoted for a pseudo-Jaffe perturber at z ≈ 0.5 (Σcrit ≈ 2.5×10⁹ M☉ kpc⁻², 1″ ≈ 6.2 kpc). Real detections sit at 10⁸·⁵–10¹⁰ M☉ and deflect by a few milliarcseconds — the slider is generous so you can see it.

Instrument 2

Cosmic web

drag to rotate · scroll to zoom
50 Mpc/h

Time

Render

What you are looking at

512,000 dark-matter particles in a periodic box 200 Mpc/h on a side, about 0.3% of the observable Universe's width. At D = 0 they sit on a perfect grid: the Universe 13.7 billion years ago, smooth to one part in 10⁵. Slide D toward 1 and each particle moves along the displacement that gravity gives it — Zel'dovich's approximation, x = q + D(t) ψ(q) — and the grid collapses into sheets, filaments and knots. Colour is the local density where the particle ends up.

Where the lenses live

The bright knots are the halos of galaxy clusters and groups; a galaxy-scale strong lens like the ones in Instrument 1 is a ~10¹³ M☉ halo sitting in one of the filaments' brighter beads. The subhalos the paper is about are far below this resolution — 10⁸–10¹⁰ M☉ crumbs orbiting inside those knots, a thousand times smaller than one cell of this grid (2.5 Mpc/h). Dark-matter theories agree on everything you can see here and disagree about the crumbs.

What is real and what is not

The initial conditions are real physics: a Gaussian random field with the ΛCDM power spectrum (Ωm = 0.3, h = 0.7, ns = 0.96, σ8 = 0.8; BBKS transfer function), seed 42. The evolution is the first-order approximation, not an N-body simulation — filaments come out slightly puffy and knots never fully collapse. IllustrisTNG or CAMELS would give you the sharp version; this one was made in numpy in eight seconds.

Lens sandbox — singular isothermal ellipsoid with external shear, optional m=3/4 multipole and pseudo-Jaffe perturber; per-pixel ray shooting in WebGL; no PSF, noise or lens light. Cosmic web — Zel'dovich displacement on an 80³ grid, rendered with three.js. Part of Dark-matter substructure from strong lensing: a systematic stress test.
